units.title: Language and Communication
units.intro: We talk about **languages** and **communication**: syllables and stress, the present tenses, the **passive**, gerunds and infinitives, and formal and informal English.

cards.title: What is this unit about?
body: This unit is about **language** and **communication**.
Communication means sharing ideas with other people: with words, pictures or movements.

cards.title: Be interested
cards.task: Have a conversation with your partner. Ask questions. Show that you are interested.

lines.text: What languages do you speak?
I speak Tigrinya and English.
That's interesting, tell me more. Do you speak English well?
Not very well. I am learning.
If you were an animal, what animal would you choose to be? Why?
A lion, because it is strong.

cards.title: The most spoken languages
body: The book shows a bar chart of six big world languages.
They are **Arabic**, **English**, **Hindi**, **Mandarin Chinese**, **Russian** and **Spanish**.
The bars show the number of speakers in millions.

cards.meaning: if not
cards.example: You should have correct pronunciation, [[otherwise]] people will not understand you.

cards.meaning: used or had by two or more people
cards.example: Knowing vocabulary is [[shared]] between meaning and pronunciation.
body: A word with a similar meaning: **joint**.

cards.meaning: facts that show something is true
cards.example: Based on this [[evidence]], you cannot come back to school.

cards.meaning: to say that something is someone's fault
cards.example: People will not understand your words and they will [[blame]] you.
body: Similar meaning: **find fault with**.

cards.meaning: to search or to discover
cards.example: In this lesson you will [[explore]] how to use the correct stress.

cards.title: What is a syllable?
body: A **syllable** is a unit of sound in a word.
A word can have one or more syllables.
Say the word aloud slowly. Then it is easier to hear the syllables.

cards.title: Syllable stress
rule: If a word has more than one syllable, one syllable is **strong** (stressed). The others are **weak**.
grandfather has 3 syllables: grand – fath – er. The first one is stressed.

examples.text: [[GRAND]]-fath-er
be-[[GIN]]
[[STRUC]]-ture
grand-[[FATH]]-er
examples.note: The first syllable of grandfather is strong.

cards.title: Clap the syllables
body: Say the word slowly and **clap** once for each syllable.
The loudest clap is the **stressed** syllable.

cards.title: Saying hello in other countries
paras: In many countries greetings are very different.
In one country people **bow** from the waist. A deeper bow shows more respect.
In another country people kiss three times on the cheeks: left, right, left.
In one country people press their noses together. This custom is called **hongi**.
In France people say *Bon jour* (Good day) and *Bon soir* (Good evening).

questions.q: What does a deep bow show?
How many times do people kiss in the second greeting?
What is the name of the greeting with noses?

cards.title: Present simple
rule: We use the **present simple** for a situation that is **always true** (a fact).
We also use it for things that **happen regularly**.

examples.text: In Italy people [[kiss]] three times.
In Japan people [[bow]].
In Japan people [[are bowing]] when they meet.
examples.fix: In Japan people [[bow]] when they meet.
examples.note: It happens regularly, so use the present simple.

cards.title: Present continuous
rule: We use the **present continuous** for an action that is **happening now**.

examples.text: She [[is kissing]] the baby.
He [[is bowing]].
Look! He [[bows]] now.

cards.q: "In Japan people bow." Why is it in the present simple?

options.A: It is a fact. It happens regularly.

cards.why: The greetings describe what people always do (p. 7).

cards.title: What do you do, what are you doing?
cards.task: Write three true sentences about you in the present simple and three in the present continuous.
model: I [[live]] in Asmara. I [[go]] to school every day. My sister [[speaks]] English well.
Now I [[am sitting]] in class. My friend [[is reading]] a book. We [[are learning]] English.

cards.title: Communication without words
paras: Communication is usually about spoken or written words. But you can also communicate without your voice.
You move your head up and down: it means "yes". You shake your head left and right: it means "no".
You move your shoulders up: it means "I don't know". You point to show where something is.
Your face also communicates. Each **facial expression** tells a different story.

questions.q: What does it mean when you shake your head left and right?
What do you do when you move your shoulders up?
questions.a: You say "I don't know" without words.

questions.q: Name two ways to communicate without talking.

cards.meaning: an idea
cards.example: The [[concept]] of communicating without words may be strange at first.

cards.meaning: showing that you do not agree
cards.example: You shake your head to mean "no" or to make a [[protest]].

cards.meaning: a movement of the hands or head that shows an idea
cards.example: These are just a few of the [[gestures]] you use every day.

cards.title: Where does English come from? (Part 1)
cards.source: English is a living language, Part 1
paras: People in Britain spoke Celtic. Then three Germanic groups came. Their languages became **Old English** (450–1100).
The Romans brought Latin words, like *cheap*, *wine* and *butter*.
In 1066 the Normans from France controlled England. Rich people spoke French. Poor people spoke English.
**Middle English** (1100–1500) had many French words, like *flower* and *blue*.
Then came **Early Modern English** (1500–1800) and printing. The first English dictionary was printed in 1604.
**Late Modern English** (1800–now) has many more words for new technology.

questions.q: Many English words come from Old English. True or false?
questions.a: True. About half of the most common words come from Old English.

questions.q: Which language did the Normans bring to England?
Does English have words from all over the world?

cards.title: Why is English spelling hard? (Part 2)
cards.source: English is a living language, Part 2
paras: English is still changing. Americans say *trash*; British people say *rubbish*.
New technology needs new words, like *Internet* and *text message*.
English has words from other languages: *zero* from Arabic, *pizza* from Italian, *jungle* from Hindi.
English is a collection of languages. So it also has many different spelling systems. That is why spelling is hard.

questions.q: Which word do Americans use for rubbish?
Which language does the word 'zero' come from?
Why is English spelling so hard?
questions.a: English is a collection of languages, so it has many spelling systems.

cards.meaning: a sign or picture that stands for something (a representation)
cards.example: This [[symbol]] '@' is called "at" in English.

cards.title: The passive voice (present)
rule: We make the passive with **to be** (am / is / are) + the **past participle** of the verb.
The object of the active sentence becomes the subject.

examples.text: Many people speak English. → English [[is spoken]] by many people.
English [[is spoke]] by many people.

cards.title: The passive voice (past)
rule: For the past simple passive, use **was / were** + the past participle.
The verb *to be* changes with the tense. The past participle stays the same.

examples.text: Rich people spoke French. → French [[was spoken]] by rich people.
Printing [[was invented]].
French [[is spoken]] by rich people in 1066.
examples.fix: French [[was spoken]] by rich people in 1066.
examples.note: 1066 is in the past: use was.

cards.title: Why do we use the passive?
body: 1. To put **important information first**: *English is spoken by many people.*
2. When **who does the action is not important**: *Printing was invented.*
Regular verbs: past participle = verb + **ed**.

cards.q: Change to the passive: "Young people invent new language."

options.A: New language is invented by young people.
options.C: Young people are invented by new language.

cards.why: The object (new language) comes first. Then is + invented (p. 13).

cards.title: How do deaf people communicate?
paras: Some people cannot hear. They are **deaf**. People can be born deaf, or become deaf after an illness or an accident.
Deaf people communicate in two ways: **speech reading** and **sign language**.
Speech reading means watching a speaker's lips and face. Only about 30% of English sounds can be seen on the lips.
Sign language uses the hands, facial expressions and body movement. Each country has its own sign language.

questions.q: What are the two ways deaf people communicate?
It is easy to understand all words with speech reading. True or false?
questions.a: False. Only about 30% of sounds can be seen on the lips.

questions.q: How do you make sign language?
questions.a: With the hands, facial expressions and body movement.

cards.meaning: to find or identify
cards.example: Many sounds of English cannot be [[detected]] on the lips.

cards.title: Verb + infinitive
rule: Some verbs are only followed by the **infinitive** (to + verb).
Verbs like this: want, ask, refuse, choose, prepare.

examples.text: I want [[to visit]] my friend.
I want [[visiting]] my friend.

cards.title: Verb + gerund (-ing)
rule: Some verbs are only followed by the **gerund** (verb + ing).
Verbs like this: enjoy, finish, miss, imagine, delay, practise, suggest, admit.

examples.text: I enjoy [[visiting]] my friend.
I enjoy [[to visit]] my friend.

cards.title: Verb + gerund or infinitive
rule: Some verbs can take **both**.
Verbs like this: like, love, hate, prefer, begin, start, continue.

examples.text: I like [[visiting]] my friend.
I like [[to visit]] my friend.
I like [[visit]] my friend.

cards.title: "Enjoy" loves -ing
body: **enjoy, finish, imagine, miss, practise** → always **-ing**.
**want, ask, choose, refuse** → always **to**.

cards.title: Formal and informal English
body: We use **formal** English with a boss, a teacher, older people or strangers.
We use **informal** English with brothers, sisters and friends.

cards.title: Apostrophe + s ('s)
rule: **'s** can show a **contraction** (a short form): it's = it is.
**'s** can also show **possession**: my friend's birthday = the birthday belongs to my friend.
Contractions are usually only used in informal language.

examples.text: [[It's]] my friend's birthday. (it is)
my [[friend's]] birthday (possession)
Good morning Sir. [[It's]] Daniel. (a formal letter)

cards.title: Informal and formal
cards.task: Talk to your friend in an informal way. Then say the same thing in a formal way.

lines.text: Hey, let's play football.
Excuse me, would you like to play football with me?
Give it here for a sec.
Please could I borrow that book?

cards.title: Write about your language
cards.task: A tourist in Eritrea wants to know about your language. Write a paragraph. Is it easy to learn? Does it use words from other languages? Then check spelling and punctuation.
model: People speak nine languages in Eritrea. My mother tongue is Tigrinya.
I think it is easy to learn for children. We also use some words from other languages, like *Internet*.
We use formal words for teachers and older people. We use informal words with our friends.

cards.title: Past simple and past continuous
rule: **Past simple**: an action that happened in the past and is finished.
**Past continuous** (was / were + -ing): a situation that continued for a time in the past.

examples.text: People [[wrote]] letters on typewriters.
While they [[were writing]], the words were printed on paper.
Yesterday people [[write]] letters.
examples.note: Yesterday = past: use the past simple.

cards.title: Future: will + verb
rule: We use **will + verb** for a situation you think will happen in the future.

examples.text: Maybe they [[will print]] without electricity.
In the future they [[will printing]] without paper.
examples.fix: In the future they [[will print]] without paper.

cards.title: Writing and printing
head: Time
Sentence from the book
rows: Now people write letters on computers.
Maybe they will print without electricity.

cards.title: Communicating: past, present and future
cards.task: Talk in your group about communicating in the past, now and in the future.

lines.text: In the past people wrote letters with a pen.
Now we write text messages on phones.
In the future, maybe we will talk to computers.

tips.text: Look for time words: every day → present simple; now, Look! → present continuous.
Passive = to be + past participle. Change the tense of 'to be' only.
enjoy + -ing, want + to.

questions.q: Which word means "if not"?
why: In the matching task, otherwise = if not (p. 4).
questions.tip: Try the word in a sentence: Hurry, otherwise you will be late.

similar.q: Which word means "shared"?

questions.q: How many syllables does "experiment" have?
why: Say it slowly: ex – per – i – ment.
That is 4 syllables (p. 4).

similar.q: How many syllables does "wonderful" have?

questions.q: Which syllable is stressed in "grandfather"?
why: grand – fath – er has 3 syllables.
The first syllable is strong (p. 5).
questions.tip: The stressed syllable is the loudest.

similar.q: Which syllable is stressed in "begin"?

questions.q: In Japan people ___ . (a fact)
why: It is always true: a fact.
Facts use the present simple (p. 7).

similar.q: In Italy people ___ three times. (a fact)

questions.q: Look! She ___ the baby.
why: Look! shows it is happening now.
Now → present continuous: is + kissing (p. 7).

similar.q: Listen! He ___ (sing).

questions.q: Change to the passive: "People speak nine languages in Eritrea."
why: The object (nine languages) comes first.
Plural, so use are + the past participle spoken (pp. 12, 21).

similar.q: Change: "Many people like pizza."
similar.a: Pizza is liked by many people.

options.A: Nine languages are spoken in Eritrea.
options.B: Nine languages is spoke in Eritrea.
options.C: Nine languages spoken people in Eritrea.

questions.q: In the past, letters ___ with a pen. (write, passive)
why: In the past → were / was.
letters is plural → were + written (p. 12).
questions.tip: Past passive: was / were + past participle.

similar.q: Computers ___ 50 years ago. (invent, passive)

questions.q: I enjoy ___ my friend.
why: enjoy is only followed by the gerund (-ing) (p. 14).

similar.q: I want ___ my friend.

questions.q: We are so pleased ___ you all to come. (ask)
why: After pleased we use to + verb (p. 14).
questions.tip: Adjective + to + verb: pleased to, ready to.

similar.q: You must get ready ___ for your class now. (leave)

questions.q: Contractions like "it's" are usually used in formal language.
why: Contractions are usually only used in informal language (p. 17).
questions.tip: Formal → write it in full: it is.

similar.q: Is "Good morning Sir" formal or informal?

questions.q: In "my friend's birthday", the 's shows ...
why: The birthday belongs to the friend.
So 's shows possession (p. 17).
questions.tip: Ask: does it mean "is"? If not, it shows possession.

similar.q: In "it's Daniel", what does 's show?

questions.q: Which language did the Normans bring to England?
why: The Normans came from France.
They brought French with them (p. 9).

similar.q: Which language did people in Britain speak first?

questions.q: Which form of English came first?
why: Old English: 450–1100.
It is the oldest form (p. 9).
questions.tip: Old → Middle → Early Modern → Late Modern.

similar.q: Which form came after Middle English?

questions.q: About how many English sounds can be seen on the lips?
why: Some people think only about 30% of English sounds can be detected on the lips (p. 15).
questions.tip: Speech reading gives only an outline of the message.

similar.q: What do deaf people watch when they speech read?

units.title: Sports and Games
units.intro: We read about **sports people** and an Afar game, learn words about the body, and use **conditionals**, **be able to** and the **present perfect**.

cards.title: Sports we like
body: The unit starts with pictures of sports.
Sports in the book: **cycling**, **boxing**, **running**, **swimming**, **football**, **basketball** and **volleyball**.
Work in a group. Choose your group's favourite sport and give a reason.

cards.title: Report your findings
cards.task: Ask another group about their favourite sport. Then report to your group.

lines.text: What is your group's favourite sport?
Our favourite sport is football, because everyone can play it.
(to her group) I found out that Group 3's favourite sport is football, because everyone can play it. They are different to our group because we chose cycling.

phrases: Our group's favourite sport is ... because ...
They are similar / different to our group because ...

cards.title: Our body systems
paras: Our body systems have different uses, but they work together.
**Skeletal system**: 206 bones, the joints and the connective tissues. They let us move and do sports.
**Muscles** are joined to our bones by tendons. They contract and relax to move our body.
**Circulatory system**: blood carries oxygen and nutrients to the cells and takes waste away.
**Respiratory system**: we breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide.
**Nervous system**: the brain controls our movements. It tells the muscles to contract.

questions.q: How many bones does our body have?
What connects skeletal muscle to our bones?
Which part of the nervous system controls voluntary movements?

cards.meaning: a part of the body that helps us to move
cards.example: Our [[muscles]] need energy to contract and relax.

cards.meaning: 1. to be loose, not contracted  2. to rest or do something enjoyable after work
cards.example: She wanted to [[relax]] after studying for a long time.

cards.meaning: 1. (nervous system) the system that controls our movements  2. worried about something
cards.example: At exam times he becomes very [[nervous]].

cards.title: Achieving dreams
paras: Natalie du Toit is a South African swimmer. She was born in Cape Town on 29 January 1984.
In February 2001 a car hit her motorcycle. Her left leg was injured and amputated at the knee.
Three months later she was back in the pool.
At 18 she won two races in world-record time at the 2002 Commonwealth Games.
In 2008 she was the first female amputee swimmer to qualify for the Olympics.
She also won many gold medals at the Paralympics.

questions.q: When and where was Natalie born?
How did Natalie lose her leg?
Natalie is the first woman amputee to qualify for the Olympics. True or false?

cards.title: Big sports events
head: Event
Who takes part
rows: all countries in the International Olympic Committee

cards.meaning: to hurt; to wound, cut, damage or harm
cards.example: In February 2001 her left leg was [[injured]].

cards.meaning: but; in spite of; on the other hand
cards.example: Her leg was amputated. [[However]], three months later she was back in the pool.

cards.title: Conjunctions
rule: **Conjunctions** join two or more words or sentences.
Examples: **and**, **but**, **or**, **however**.

examples.text: Bed [[and]] breakfast.
I played [[but]] she studied.
You can play basketball [[or]] volleyball.
She ran very fast [[and]] she didn't catch the bus.
examples.fix: She ran very fast [[but]] she didn't catch the bus.
examples.note: The two ideas are opposite, so use but.

cards.title: Prepositions of place
rule: **Prepositions of place** tell us where something is.
Examples: between, in, in front of, next to, behind, opposite, beside, on.

examples.text: The shop is [[opposite]] the stadium.
The ball is [[between]] the two boxes.
The ball is [[between]] the box.

cards.title: Where is the ball?
body: Look at each picture. Say where the ball is.

cards.title: How to play Snakes and Ladders
body: Players: 4 to 6. You need a board, a piece for each player and one **die**.
Throw the die. Move forward the number on the die.
Land at the bottom of a **ladder**: go up to the top.
Land on the tail of a **snake**: go down to its head.
The first player to reach square 90 wins.

cards.title: Zero conditional
rule: **If clause + main clause**, both in the **present simple**.
It shows what always happens when something else happens.

examples.text: If water [[boils]], it [[evaporates]].
If a player [[gets]] 6, they also [[have]] another turn.
If water [[boil]], it evaporates.

cards.title: First conditional
rule: **If clause** in the present simple + **main clause** with will + verb.
It shows something is possible if something else happens.

examples.text: If you [[run]] fast, you [[will catch]] the bus.
If they [[pay]] the money, we [[will give]] them the cake.
If you [[will run]] fast, you will catch the bus.
examples.fix: If you [[run]] fast, you will catch the bus.
examples.note: No will in the if clause.

cards.title: No 'will' after 'if'
body: The **if** part uses the present simple. **will** goes in the other part.

cards.title: Working hard
paras: Yohannes Zemichael was born in Asmara in 1972. He was one of the best Eritrean footballers.
In 1989 he joined the Police Football Team (now Altahrir). He also played 17 international games.
In 1992 he was named star in the championships in Asmara. He was able to score 10 goals.
He joined the Hilal Sport Club of Sudan. He became the second Eritrean professional footballer.
In 2007 CAF gave him a special medal for the best Eritrean footballer of 1957–2007.
He died in Sudan on 25 February 1994, after an illness.

questions.q: When was Yohannes born?
Which club did he join in Sudan?
Who was the first Eritrean professional footballer?
questions.a: Ahmed Abdella (in the United Arab Emirates, 1980s).

cards.meaning: a strong feeling of interest and enjoyment about something
cards.example: Yohannes loved football and played with great [[enthusiasm]].

cards.meaning: to shout with happiness; a shout of happiness
cards.example: His fans [[cheered]] when he showed his great skills.

cards.title: be able to (ability)
rule: **be + able to** + main verb shows ability. It means *can* or *could*.
The helping verb (am / is / are / was) goes with the subject. The main verb does not change.
For negative, question or past, change the **be** part.

examples.text: He [[was able to]] score 10 goals.
[[Is]] she [[able to]] finish on time?
He [[is not able to]] complete the picture.
They are able to [[climbed]] the tree.
examples.fix: They are able to [[climb]] the tree.
examples.note: The main verb does not change.

cards.pattern: am / is / are / was + able to + [[verb]]

cards.title: A model paragraph
cards.task: Write a paragraph of 6–8 sentences. Compare two sports people: where they come from, their sport, prizes and achievements.
model: [[Here I am going to compare two well-known sports people.]] They are called Natalie du Toit and Yohannes Zemichael.
Natalie was born in South Africa in 1984. She won many gold medals in swimming. She is best known for being the first amputee to qualify for the Olympics.
Yohannes, on the other hand, was born in 1972 in Asmara, Eritrea. He was one of the best Eritrean footballers.
In 1992, he was named star by scoring 10 goals in the championships held in Asmara. He is the second Eritrean professional footballer.
phrases: Here I am going to compare ...
body: This is part of the book's own model paragraph (p. 39).

cards.title: The topic sentence
body: A **topic sentence** shows what a paragraph will be about.
It is usually the **first sentence**.
The next sentences develop it further.

cards.title: Traditional games are fun
paras: Daka is a traditional game of Afar children. They play it at night in the moonlight, on flat ground.
The children make two equal teams. They choose a judge, called **Inayta**.
The judge throws a small white stick or a goat's bone far away. The teams listen to the sound and run to find it.
The finder shouts "Ali yo le" (I have found it!) and runs to the judge.
If the other team touches the stick, the game is **cancelled** and starts again.
The first team with ten points wins.

questions.q: What time is Daka played?
"Ali yo le" means "it is behind you". True or false?
questions.a: False. It means "I have found it".

questions.q: What happens if the other team touches the stick?
questions.a: The game stops and they play again.

cards.meaning: to stop an event from happening
cards.example: The game is [[cancelled]] and it starts all over again.

cards.meaning: treating everyone equally
cards.example: The judge judges in a [[fair]] way.

cards.title: Present perfect
rule: Use **have / has + past participle** for:
1. an action **completed recently**;
2. an action that started in the past and **still continues**.

examples.text: She [[has just finished]] writing the letter.
I [[have lived]] in Asmara for my whole life.
I [[have finished]] the letter yesterday.
examples.note: yesterday is a definite time: use the past simple.

cards.title: Time words
body: Do **not** use definite time words with the present perfect: *yesterday, two years ago, an hour ago*.
Use them with the past simple and past continuous.

cards.meaning: to trust or depend on someone
cards.example: We trust him. You can [[rely]] on what he is saying.

cards.meaning: to become well again after an illness
cards.example: My friend is [[recovering]] from his illness.

cards.meaning: to move backwards and forwards
cards.example: He likes [[swinging]] the baby in his arms.

a word that tells the place: between, behind, beside
if + present simple, present simple
if + present simple, will + verb
the first sentence that shows what a paragraph is about
have / has + past participle
a person who has lost an arm or a leg
sports events for athletes with a disability
the bones, joints and connective tissues
the system for breathing

tips.text: No will after if: If you run, you will catch the bus.
be able to: only the 'be' part changes.
yesterday / ago → past simple, not present perfect.

questions.q: How many bones does our body have?
why: The text says our body has 206 bones (p. 24).
questions.tip: Skeletal system = bones + joints + connective tissues.

similar.q: Which system carries oxygen in the blood?

questions.q: "At exam times he becomes very nervous." Here nervous means ...
why: nervous also means to worry about something (p. 26).
questions.tip: Some words have two meanings. Look at the sentence.

similar.q: "She wanted to relax after studying." relax means ...

questions.q: How did Natalie du Toit lose her leg?
why: A car hit her while she was riding her motorcycle (p. 27).

similar.q: Where was Natalie born?

questions.q: My sister fell from the bicycle and ___ her right arm.
why: injure = hurt. Past: injured (p. 30).

similar.q: Last night I didn't sleep well; ___ I went to school on time.

questions.q: The man is very old; ___ he climbed the mountain.
why: The two ideas are surprising together, so use however (p. 31).

similar.q: Cycling ___ swimming are my favourite sports.

questions.q: The ball is on the left of the box, very near it. The ball is ___ the box.
why: beside = next to (p. 31).
questions.tip: between needs two things; behind = at the back.

similar.q: The ball is in the middle of two boxes. It is ___ the boxes.

questions.q: If water boils, it ___ . (evaporate)
why: Zero conditional: present simple in both parts.
water = it → evaporates (p. 34).

questions.tip: Check three parts: are + able to + climb.

similar.a: Is she able to finish on time?

options.B: They are able climb the tall tree.

why: "Ali yo le" means "I have found it".
"Ali hara fan" means "it is behind you" (p. 40).
questions.tip: Read the two Afar phrases carefully.

why: fair = treating everyone equally (p. 41).

why: Present perfect: has + past participle (finished).
No definite time like yesterday (p. 42).

units.title: Changes
units.intro: We talk about the **changes** of adolescence, **friendship** and saying **no** to peer pressure. Grammar: adverbs of frequency, reflexive pronouns, articles, the **second conditional**, modal verbs and plurals.

cards.title: Changes
paras: From birth to adulthood our body and our mind change a lot.
In **adolescence** the physical change is very fast. Hair grows under the arms. Some teenagers get spots on their face.
Girls' breasts grow and their hips get wider. Boys' shoulders and muscles get broader, and their voices get deeper.
Teenagers sometimes feel **embarrassed** about these changes. Their **mood** can change quickly.
They start to become independent of their parents. Parents often find this stage **tough**.

questions.q: What do teenagers feel embarrassed about?
questions.a: The changes in their body, for example spots or a deeper voice.

questions.q: Girls' voices deepen in adolescence. True or false?
Why do parents find adolescence difficult?
questions.a: Teenagers' moods change, they become independent and sometimes lie.

cards.meaning: how you feel at a time
cards.example: He was not in a good [[mood]]. (He didn't feel OK.)

cards.meaning: difficult
cards.example: The homework is too [[tough]] to do myself. I need help.

cards.meaning: ashamed; shy about something
cards.example: The boy was [[embarrassed]] by his wrong doings.

cards.meaning: to discuss a problem to agree
cards.example: The girl [[negotiated]] with her father about going out.

cards.title: What good friends do
head: Quality
Meaning (from the book)
rows: You can trust your friends to tell you the truth.
They respect your feelings and opinions.
They accept mistakes and say 'I am sorry.'
They will always be there when you need them.
They don't just tell you what you want to hear.
They help you when things go wrong.
They don't ask you to do things that will harm you.

cards.meaning: always there for you; dependable
cards.example: If your friends stand by your side when you are in trouble, they are [[loyal]].

cards.meaning: you can trust them with a secret
cards.example: If your friends don't tell your secrets to anyone, they are [[trustworthy]].

cards.meaning: ready to excuse your mistakes
cards.example: If your friends excuse you for your mistakes, they are [[forgiving]].

cards.title: Teens' views
paras: **Senait** (18) has been friends with Aman for 3 years. She trusts him. He never judges her. He supports her decisions.
**Abraham** (17) says his father is very strict. He never listens to his problems. Abraham never tells him the truth.
**Asha** (18) does not believe what her friend Kini says. He never respects her family. He often comes to their home drunk.

questions.q: What does Senait like about Aman?
questions.a: She can talk to him about everything; he never judges her and he supports her.

questions.q: Kini respects Asha's family. True or false?
questions.a: False. He never respects her family.

questions.q: Does Abraham like his father?
questions.a: No. His father never listens to him and embarrasses him.

cards.title: Where does the adverb go?
rule: 1. With most verbs, the adverb goes **before** the main verb.
2. With the verb **be**, the adverb goes **after** the verb.

examples.text: I [[always]] talk to him at school.
Kini is [[always]] late for school.
I talk [[always]] to him at school.
examples.fix: I [[always]] talk to him at school.

examples.text: Kini [[always]] is late.

cards.title: Be comes first
body: With **be** (am, is, are): the verb first, then the adverb: *He is never late.*
Other verbs: the adverb first: *He never comes late.*

cards.title: People I like
cards.task: Write a paragraph of 6 to 8 sentences about a person you like or dislike. Why? What does he or she do? Then check your partner's spelling and punctuation.
model: I like my friend Aman. He is always honest with me. He never judges me.
He usually helps me with my homework. We sometimes go for a walk after school. He is a loyal friend.

cards.title: Poor Asha (Part one)
paras: Ali's wife Zeineb died a year ago. He has three young children.
The village elders tell Ali to marry again. At first Ali **rejects** the idea. Then he lets the elders decide.
The elders go to Salih's house. They ask for his daughter Asha to marry Ali.
Asha is 18. She is in Grade 10 and she is very good at school.
Her father is happy. Ali is rich and has a good **personality**.

questions.q: reject means ...
personality means ...
How old is Asha and what grade is she in?

cards.title: Poor Asha (Part two)
paras: The family talks to Asha. Her brothers say the men should decide her future.
Asha says: "Dad, give me a chance to decide for myself. I am old enough."
Her father **alters** his thinking: "We were wrong and she is right."
He says they will wait until Asha finishes her university studies.

questions.q: What does Asha ask her father?
questions.a: To give her a chance to decide for herself.

questions.q: What does her father decide in the end?
questions.a: Asha can decide; they will wait until she finishes university.

cards.meaning: to change
cards.example: I have [[altered]] my thinking. We were wrong and she is right.

cards.title: Reflexive pronouns
rule: **Reflexive pronouns** show that the action is done by the person already named.
They end in **-self** (one person) or **-selves** (more than one).

examples.text: I made the cake [[myself]].
We are old enough to do everything by [[ourselves]].
The girls can do it [[herself]].

cards.title: Bad teenagers
paras: **Peer pressure** is influence by people of your own age.
Bad teenagers can push good teenagers to do wrong things, like drinking alcohol or smoking.
Hassen's friends told him to smoke. He said no: smoking damages your health and appearance.
Shewit told her boyfriend she didn't want sex before marriage. Their relationship ended after a few months.

questions.q: What is peer pressure?
questions.a: Influence by people of your own age.

questions.q: Did Hassen accept his friends' invitation to smoke?
questions.a: No. It makes him sick and damages health.

cards.title: Articles: a, an, the, no article
rule: **a / an**: one thing, the first time we talk about it (**an** before a vowel sound).
**the**: a thing we already know, or the only one (the highest).
**no article**: things in general, like water.

examples.text: Bereket lives in [[a]] small house. [[The]] house doesn't have a window.
It is [[the]] highest mountain in Eritrea.
The teacher said [[a]] elephant can swim.
examples.fix: The teacher said [[an]] elephant can swim.
examples.note: elephant starts with a vowel sound: an.

lessons.title: Saying no and the second conditional

cards.title: Steps to say 'No' to negative peer pressure
cards.source: Steps To Say 'NO' To Negative Peer Pressure
paras: Saying no to friends is not easy. The book gives some ways.
Say "I know." You know what is important for you. Say "Not now."
Say "I can make my own decision." Say "My parents trust me. I don't want to disappoint them."
Say "If you were my friend, you wouldn't pressure me." Real friends never push you to do harmful things.

questions.q: Is it easy to say no to negative peer pressure?
questions.a: No. You need to know exactly how to say no.

questions.q: Do real friends encourage their friends to do something wrong?

cards.title: Second conditional
rule: **If** + past simple, **would** + verb.
Use it for **unreal** situations, or things we **don't expect** to happen.

examples.text: If you [[were]] my friend, you [[wouldn't pressure]] me.
If I [[won]] some money, I [[would visit]] the Egyptian Pyramids.
If I [[would have]] the money, I would buy a car.
examples.fix: If I [[had]] the money, I would buy a car.
examples.note: No would in the if clause.

cards.title: Give advice (model)
task: Choose a problem. For example: What would you say if your friends asked you to smoke?
model: If my friends asked me to smoke cigarettes, I would say no. I would reject them because I know what is most important for me.
I would advise them that smoking is bad for our health. It damages our lungs and teeth.
body: This is the book's own example (p. 62).

lessons.title: Asking for advice and modal verbs

cards.title: Teenage pregnancy (Parts one and three)
paras: Ruta is in Grade 10. At a wedding her boyfriend Mussie gave her a lot of alcohol. She didn't say no.
Later she found she was pregnant. She felt guilty and didn't know what to tell her mother.
She went to the school counsellor, Gebru. He said: "Good communication is essential for solving problems."
"You ought to listen to other people's points of view. You ought not to get angry."
In the end Ruta decides to tell her parents and Mussie.

questions.q: Why did Ruta go to Gebru?
What ought young people to do when a problem occurs?
questions.a: Deal with it as it occurs.

questions.q: What does Ruta decide at the end?
questions.a: To tell her parents and Mussie and listen to them.

cards.title: should / ought to (advice)
rule: **Should** and **ought to** have similar meanings. We use them to give advice.
The verb after them is the base form.

examples.text: We [[should]] respect our parents.
We [[ought to]] respect our parents.
You ought [[listen]] to other people.
examples.fix: You [[ought to listen]] to other people.

cards.title: must / have to (strong)
rule: **Must** and **have to** are much stronger than should and ought to.
*You must stop smoking.* = a command. You have no choice.

examples.text: You [[must]] stop smoking.
Helen [[has to]] eat fish and drink milk. She is seriously sick.
You [[must to]] stop smoking.

cards.meaning: to think about something and judge it
cards.example: Be willing to hear and [[evaluate]] different opinions.

cards.title: Soft or strong?
body: **should, ought to** = advice (soft).
**must, have to** = command (strong).

cards.title: Regular plurals
rule: Most nouns: add **s** (parents, friends).
Ending in y: change **y** to **i** and add **es** (lady → ladies, party → parties).
Some nouns add **es** (box → boxes, church → churches).

examples.text: two [[boxes]]
many [[parties]]
three [[ladys]]

cards.title: Irregular plurals
rule: Irregular plurals have **no rule**. Learn them.

examples.text: one sheep → two [[sheep]]
one child → two [[children]]
one woman → two [[women]]
one foot → two [[foots]]

lessons.title: because, so that and mind maps

cards.title: because and so that
rule: **because** + the **reason** for the action.
**so that** + the **purpose** of the action.

examples.text: I study French [[because]] I like the French culture.
The teacher spoke slowly [[so that]] the students could write everything down.
Ruta went to the counsellor [[so that]] she needed advice.
examples.fix: Ruta went to the counsellor [[because]] she needed advice.

units.title: Science and Technology
units.intro: We read about simple **technology**, **biodiversity**, and the scientists E. O. Wilson and Marie Curie. Grammar: **as** and **since**, the **past perfect**, -ed sounds and spelling.

cards.title: Technology for the other 90%
cards.source: Technology for the other 90% / 5 new technologies
paras: Nearly 90% of the world's people can't get things that the richest 10% think are normal.
A competition showed simple technology that helps people in developing countries.
The **LifeStraw** is a drinking tube. People can safely drink unclean water through it.
The **Q-Drum** looks like the letter Q. Children can pull 50 litres of water with a rope.
**PermaNet** is a mosquito net that kills the mosquitoes too. It lasts several years.
**One Laptop per Child** is a cheap, lightweight computer. **Portable Light** is cloth that gives light.

questions.q: The LifeStraw only lets people drink clean water. True or false?
questions.a: False. People can safely drink unclean water with it.

questions.q: Is it easy for children to pull the Q-Drum?
If you wash the PermaNet you lose the insecticide. True or false?
questions.a: False. It can be washed many times.

questions.q: Which word in the text means 'not heavy'?

cards.title: Five technologies
head: Technology
What it does
rows: a cheap computer for every child
light where there is no electricity
people can safely drink unclean water
a mosquito net that kills mosquitoes

cards.meaning: to invent
cards.example: A Danish company has [[devised]] a special drinking tube.

cards.meaning: evidence
cards.example: The company has produced the [[proof]] that people can safely drink unclean water.

cards.title: Which technology is the most important?
cards.task: Rank the 5 technologies from 1 to 5. Give your reasons.

lines.text: I think the LifeStraw is number 1, because dirty water carries diseases.
I agree. Number 2 is PermaNet, because malaria kills millions of people.
What about the laptop?
It is important for education, but clean water comes first.

cards.meaning: a big variety of different species
cards.example: E. O. Wilson wants people to protect [[biodiversity]].

cards.meaning: the place where a species lives, feeds and produces its young
cards.example: Destroying [[habitats]] is a cause of biodiversity loss.

cards.meaning: when a complete species has disappeared from the planet
cards.example: All the dinosaurs became [[extinct]].

cards.meaning: almost disappearing
cards.example: Many species are [[endangered]].

cards.title: A sixth extinction
cards.source: A Sixth Extinction – the Loss of Earth's Biodiversity
paras: Scientists have evidence of five big extinctions of life on earth.
The last one was about 65 million years ago. A **meteorite** (a giant rock from space) crashed in Mexico.
The sky became dark for many years. All the dinosaurs became extinct.
Now scientists say a **sixth extinction** has started. This time it is caused by **human activity**.
Today 23% of mammals and 23% of birds are threatened with extinction.

questions.q: How many big extinctions has the earth had?
When was the fifth big extinction? What happened?
questions.a: About 65 million years ago; a meteorite crashed onto the earth.

questions.q: Why is the sixth extinction different?
questions.a: It is caused by human activity.

cards.title: HIPPO
body: The biologist E. O. Wilson made the word **HIPPO** to remember the main causes of biodiversity loss.
Think of a large, sad hippopotamus!

letters.m: species that come in and eat or compete

cards.q: Fishermen pull big nets along the sea bottom and catch a lot of fish. Which letter is this?
cards.why: Catching too many fish is overharvesting (p. 79).

cards.meaning: to damage completely, so nothing remains
cards.example: People [[destroy]] habitats for agriculture and fuel.

cards.meaning: something that is burned to give power or heat
cards.example: People cut down the trees for [[fuel]].

cards.title: Pronouncing -ed
rule: The sound of **-ed** depends on the last **sound** of the verb, not the spelling.
After a **t** or **d** sound, say **/id/** (an extra syllable): end → end-ed.
After other sounds, do **not** add an 'i' or 'e' sound.

examples.text: start → [[start-id]]
persuade → [[persuad-id]]
fail → [[faild]]
fail → [[fail-id]]
examples.note: No extra syllable: fail does not end in t or d.

lessons.title: E. O. Wilson, as and since

cards.title: The Father of 'Biodiversity'
paras: Edward Osborne Wilson is a famous biologist. He made the word **biodiversity**: 'bio' = life, 'diversity' = variety.
He was born in 1929 in Alabama, USA. As a boy he loved snakes, so people called him 'snake'.
At 7 he was blinded in one eye. So he studied small creatures: ants. People call him 'Dr Ant'.
He has worked at Harvard University since 1951. He wrote *Biophilia* (1984) and *The Diversity of Life* (1992).
In 2007 he started the **Encyclopedia of Life** on the Internet, with a page for every species.

questions.q: In which science is E. O. Wilson an expert?
Why is he called 'Dr Ant'?
questions.a: He is the world's leading expert on ants.

questions.q: Is the Encyclopedia of Life a book or on the Internet?

cards.title: Timeline of E. O. Wilson's life

steps.text: At 7 he was blinded in one eye.
1992: he wrote The Diversity of Life.
2007: he started the Encyclopedia of Life.

cards.title: as = because
rule: **as** can be used instead of **because**. It gives a reason.

examples.text: [[As]] he was tired, he went to bed early.
You should be in the school team [[as]] you are a good footballer.
He studied ants [[as]] he couldn't easily study large animals.
As he was tired, [[so]] he went to bed.
examples.fix: [[As]] he was tired, he went to bed.

cards.title: since (time)
rule: **since** can show the **time something started**.
It is often used with the **present perfect**.

examples.text: He [[has lost]] a lot of weight [[since]] he started taking exercise.
She [[has drunk]] a lot of coffee [[since]] she arrived.
He [[works]] at Harvard since 1951.

cards.meaning: to frighten; (scared) frightened
cards.example: The old lady was too [[scared]] to open the door.

cards.title: The life of E. O. Wilson
cards.task: Write two short paragraphs: an introduction, then events from the timeline.
model: E. O. Wilson is probably the most important biologist in the world. He wants people to protect biodiversity.
He was born in 1929. When he was 7, he was blinded in one eye. In 1951 he joined Harvard University. In 1992 he wrote his most famous book.

lessons.title: Marie Curie and the past perfect

cards.title: A wonderful woman
paras: Marie Curie was a physicist and chemist. She was born in Poland in 1867.
She moved to France in 1891. In 1895 she married Pierre Curie.
In 1911 she won a Nobel Prize for her work in radioactivity and for discovering 2 new elements.
During the war (1914–1918) she trained 150 nurses to do x-rays for hurt soldiers.
She died in 1934. The elements she worked with were dangerous. They had given her cancer.

questions.q: Where did she come from?
What is she famous for?
questions.a: Her work in radioactivity and discovering 2 new elements.

questions.q: Why did she die?
questions.a: The dangerous elements had given her cancer.

cards.title: Past perfect
rule: **had + past participle**.
Use it to show that one past action happened **before** another.

examples.text: She won a Nobel Prize in 1911. She [[had married]] Pierre Curie in 1895.
They [[had given]] her cancer.
She trained nurses in 1914. She [[has won]] a Nobel Prize in 1911.
examples.fix: She trained nurses in 1914. She [[had won]] a Nobel Prize in 1911.
examples.note: The earlier action: had + past participle.

cards.title: What did you do first?
cards.task: Tell your partner about yesterday using the past perfect.

lines.text: Yesterday afternoon I played football.
Yesterday morning I had studied English.

cards.title: Plankton
cards.source: Plankton are the base of the food chain in water
paras: Plankton are very small organisms. They live in rivers, lakes and the sea. They **float** near the surface.
They are the bottom of the **food chain**. Big plankton eat small plankton. Small fish eat big plankton.
Bigger fish eat small fish, and humans eat the big fish.
Some plankton make gasses that help to make clouds. So they affect the climate.

questions.q: Where do plankton live?
questions.a: In fresh water rivers and lakes, and the sea.

questions.q: Can plankton influence the climate? How?
questions.a: Yes. Some make gasses that influence the making of clouds.

cards.title: Bees and fungi
cards.source: We depend on bees for food / Fungi keep plants and trees alive
paras: About 250,000 kinds of flowering plants need bees for **pollination**. 70% of food crops need bees and other insects.
Bee populations are getting smaller, because we use more land for agriculture.
Fungi have a bad reputation, but very few cause problems. Plants get food and water through fungi and their roots.
Medicines like penicillin are made from fungi.

questions.q: What percentage of food crops depend on bees and other insects?
Most fungi are poisonous. True or false?
questions.a: False. Very few fungi cause problems.

questions.q: Name a medicine made from fungi.

cards.meaning: to stay on the water without going down
cards.example: Wood [[floats]] in water but rock does not.

cards.title: Our group's decision
cards.task: In your group, choose the most valuable species. Give two or three reasons.

lines.text: We think bees are the most valuable species.
First, 70% of food crops need bees and other insects.
Second, without bees there will be no more beautiful flowers.

phrases: We think ... is the most valuable species.

cards.title: Internet or space travel?
paras: Halima likes the Internet. Communication is convenient and people can get useful information.
John says people spend less time talking face-to-face. Also anybody can put anything on the Internet.
John likes manned space flight. We can learn a lot and do experiments in space.
Halima says it is very expensive. A manned vehicle costs at least a hundred times more than an unmanned one.
She thinks we should spend our money on this beautiful planet.

questions.q: What is one disadvantage of the Internet that John gives?
questions.a: People talk less face-to-face / there is no control of information.

questions.q: How much more does a manned space vehicle cost?
questions.a: At least a hundred times more than an unmanned one.

cards.title: Advantages and disadvantages
head: Advantage
Disadvantage
rows: less face-to-face talk; no real control
we learn a lot; experiments in space

cards.title: Adding -ed and -ing
rule: Verb ends in **e**: add **d** (hope → hoped).
One **e**: drop the e and add **ing** (move → moving).
Two e's: just add ing (agree → agreeing).

examples.text: move → [[moved]], [[moving]]
agree → [[agreeing]]
move → [[moveing]]

cards.title: Doubling the last consonant
rule: Double the last consonant when the word ends in **one vowel + one consonant** AND that syllable is **stressed**.
Examples: stop → stopped, sit → sitting, begin → beginning, prefer → preferred.

examples.text: win → [[winning]]
stop → [[stopped]]
eat → [[eatting]]

units.title: Everyone is Different
units.intro: We talk about how **people are different**, about **bullying** and **disabilities**, and read about Helen Keller. Grammar: although / however, can / be able to, **comparisons**, relative clauses and like.

cards.title: Find differences and similarities
cards.task: Talk to your partner. Find out how you are different and how you are the same.

lines.text: What do you like doing best?
I like playing football. And you?
I like reading. What do you want to be when you grow up?
A pilot.
What are you like as a person?
I am quite shy, but I am kind.

phrases: What do you like doing best?
What do you want to be when you grow up?
What are you like as a person?

cards.title: Everyone is different
paras: People differ in many ways. Some are tall and thin, some are short and heavy.
If we were all the same, life would be boring.
Differences in height and weight don't matter at all.
What matters most is how you behave towards other people: your **conduct**.
Good behaviour helps you to be a friend that everyone wants.

questions.q: Your behaviour towards other people doesn't matter at all. True or false?
questions.a: False. Your conduct matters the most.

questions.q: Does it matter if you are shorter or taller than other people?
questions.a: No, these differences don't matter at all.

questions.q: What does conduct mean?

cards.meaning: behaviour
cards.example: It is your [[conduct]] towards other people that matters the most.

cards.title: although
rule: **although** joins two **contrasting** (differing) ideas.
After although we use a **subject + verb**. It can start the sentence or go in the middle.

examples.text: [[Although]] it rained a lot, they enjoyed their holiday.
They enjoyed their holiday [[although]] it rained a lot.
[[Although]] it rained a lot, [[but]] they enjoyed it.
examples.fix: [[Although]] it rained a lot, they enjoyed it.

cards.title: however
rule: **however** also joins two contrasting ideas.
Use a **semicolon (;)** before it and a **comma** after it.

examples.text: It rained a lot[[; however,]] they had fun.
We had planned everything carefully[[; however,]] a lot of things went wrong.
It rained a lot [[however]] they had fun.
examples.fix: It rained a lot[[; however,]] they had fun.

cards.q: "___ there was a lot of noise, I was able to sleep."
cards.why: A subject and verb follow, and the ideas contrast: although (p. 99).

lessons.title: What makes people unique? Using a dictionary

cards.title: What makes people unique?
paras: People from towns and people from the countryside have different backgrounds and life styles.
Your upbringing, your friends, your books and your songs build your **personality**.
**Modest** people are quiet and often shy. They are not arrogant.
Everyone is born with **potential**: an inner driving force to do something.
**Sensible** people are practical. They think a lot and give judgment based on reasons and facts.

questions.q: Modest people are ...
Sensible people are ...
Name some factors that shape our personality.

cards.meaning: quiet, reserved and not proud
cards.example: [[Modest]] people are reserved and most of the time shy.

cards.meaning: practical and reasonable
cards.example: People who are practical and do things after a lot of thought are called [[sensible]] people.

cards.title: Alphabetical order
body: First list the words.
Look at the first letter. If the first letters are the same, look at the **first letters that are different**.
All the words in a dictionary are in alphabetical order.

cards.q: Which list is in alphabetical order?
cards.why: de-l comes before de-n, and de-n before de-s (p. 101).

cards.title: One word, many meanings
body: In a dictionary one word can have several meanings.
*delay* can be a verb and a noun.
Choose the meaning that goes with your sentence (the context).

cards.title: Are you being bullied? (Part 1)
paras: Bullying is **not** normal. If you are bullied, it is not your fault.
Don't feel **guilty**, but don't ignore it.
Common forms: making fun of someone, damaging their things, leaving someone out, spreading bad information, beating someone.
People are bullied because of their weight, looks, race, religion or social background.

questions.q: Bullying is normal. True or false?
Name two common forms of bullying.
questions.a: For example: name calling, leaving someone out of a group.

questions.q: People are sometimes bullied because of their looks. True or false?

cards.meaning: sickening
cards.example: We sometimes ignore [[disgusting]] behaviour because we hope it will go away.

cards.meaning: responsible for a wrong doing
cards.example: If you are being bullied, you shouldn't feel [[guilty]].

cards.title: can and be able to (ability)
rule: We use **can** to say that something is possible, or that somebody has the ability to do something.
**be able to** has the same meaning, but can is more usual.

examples.text: I [[can]] ride a bicycle.
Nahom [[was able to]] pass his exam.
[[Can]] you speak English? Yes, I can.
I [[can to]] ride a bicycle.

cards.title: Ways of helping yourself (Part 2)
paras: Always tell someone you trust, like your teacher or your parents.
Until then you can: stay calm and walk away, act confidently, and keep your friends around you.
Don't be silent. You deserve to go in and out of school freely.

questions.q: You must ignore the fact that you are being bullied. True or false?
If your friend is being bullied, what should you do?
questions.a: Tell a parent or a teacher.

cards.title: How to write a description
body: 1. Choose a topic: an object, a person, a place or an event.
2. Write short notes: colour, size, feelings.
3. Start with a **topic sentence**.
4. For people: appearance, behaviour, clothes and hair.
5. Use different **adjectives**.

cards.title: A descriptive paragraph
cards.task: Choose a person, a place or an object. Describe it so your reader can see what you see.
model: [[My grandmother is a small, kind woman.]] She has short grey hair and warm brown eyes.
She usually wears a long white dress. She is always calm and patient.
When she tells stories, her voice is soft and her hands move slowly.
body: The first sentence is the topic sentence.

cards.title: Comparatives
rule: One syllable: add **-er** (old → older, late → later).
Ending in -y: **-ier** (heavy → heavier).
Longer words: **more** (more expensive).

examples.text: It is [[cheaper]] to go by bus than by taxi.
This basket is [[heavier]] than the other.
This book is [[expensiver]] than that one.
examples.fix: This book is [[more expensive]] than that one.

cards.title: Superlatives
rule: One syllable: **the + -est** (the shortest).
Ending in -y: **the -iest** (the easiest).
Longer words: **the most** (the most careful).

examples.text: What is [[the longest]] river in Eritrea?
English is [[the easiest]] subject.
She is [[the most kind]] teacher.
examples.note: kind has one syllable: the kindest.

cards.title: as ... as
rule: Use **as + adjective + as** to compare two **equal** things.
not as ... as = less.

examples.text: This book is [[as good as]] that book.
I'm [[not as tall as]] my brother.
I'm not as tall [[than]] my brother.
examples.fix: I'm not as tall [[as]] my brother.

cards.meaning: strong and effective
cards.example: If it is strong and effective, it is [[potent]].

cards.title: Writing about statistics
cards.task: Look at statistics about schools. Write sentences with comparisons.
model: Between 2000 and 2007 the percentage of young men who can read is [[greater than]] the percentage of young women.
body: This is the book's example sentence (p. 111).

lessons.title: Disabilities, relative clauses and Helen Keller

cards.title: Reflexive pronouns (review)
rule: Add **-self** or **-selves** to the pronoun.
Use it when the subject does the action to itself, or for **emphasis**.

examples.text: Kaleb cut [[himself]] when he was shaving.
She taught [[herself]] to play the piano.
Rahwa fell down and hurt [[himself]].

cards.title: Overcoming disabilities in school life
paras: A disability may limit a person's hearing, sight, speech or mental function. Many disabilities cannot be seen.
A disability shouldn't stop someone from going to school or doing any kind of work.
People with disabilities have equal rights. They can learn with their peers.
Wheelchairs, crutches and accessible buildings help. Students should **volunteer** to help if necessary.

questions.q: Almost all disabilities are visible. True or false?
What does volunteer mean?
questions.a: an unpaid helper (to help without pay).

cards.title: Relative clauses
rule: A **relative clause** gives information about a noun. It starts with who, which, that, where or when.
**Defining**: important information, no commas. **Non-defining**: extra information, between commas.
Use **who** for people and **which / that** for things.

examples.text: This is the house [[that I told you about]].
My family[[, who I love very much,]] are my best friends.
Our English teacher [[, which is very kind,]] has come back.
examples.fix: Our English teacher[[, who is very kind,]] has come back.

cards.title: Helen Keller
paras: At 19 months Helen had a high fever. It made her deaf and blind.
She made sixty signs with her hands to 'talk' to her family.
Her teacher, Anne Sullivan, spelled words into Helen's hand. Helen also learned to read **braille**: dots for blind readers.
In college she wrote her first book, *The Story of My Life*.
She was successful because of her **determination** and her teacher's help.

questions.q: What caused Helen's disabilities?
What is braille used for?
questions.a: Reading for blind people, by feeling dots.

questions.q: Why was Helen successful?
questions.a: Because she was determined, and her teacher helped her.

cards.meaning: to give money or time
cards.example: She [[contributed]] a lot of money from her books to help the disabled.

cards.meaning: to demand something firmly
cards.example: Anne Sullivan [[insisted]] on teaching Helen everything.

cards.title: like as a verb
rule: **like** is not used in the -ing form, even for present events.
It always has an object.

examples.text: "What do you think of the house?" "I [[like]] it."
She [[likes]] chocolate.
I [[am liking]] the house.

cards.title: like = similar to
rule: **like** also means *similar to*.
*What is she like?* asks about a person's character. *look like* is about appearance.

examples.text: He [[looks just like]] his mother.
"What is your sister [[like]]?" "She is a wonderful girl."
He [[looks just like as]] his mother.

body: The book calls this 'like as an adverb' (p. 118).

glossary.meaning: behaviour
a difference between two ideas
a person's character
hurting or frightening someone again and again
older, heavier, more expensive
the oldest, the easiest, the most careful
a part of a sentence that starts with who, which, that, where
a condition that may limit hearing, sight, speech or mental function
a reading system of dots for blind people
not giving up

-er / more ... than; the -est / the most.
Commas → non-defining clause (extra information).

questions.q: What does 'conduct' mean in the text?
why: The text says your conduct towards other people matters most (p. 98).
questions.tip: Read the sentence before: 'how one person reacts to another'.

similar.q: According to the text, what matters most?
similar.a: how you behave towards other people

questions.q: I can't get it right ___ I tried hard.
why: Contrasting ideas, followed by subject + verb: although (p. 99).

similar.q: My mother loves chocolate ___ it makes her sick.

questions.q: I couldn't find a solution; ___, I approached the problem carefully.
why: After a semicolon, with a comma after: however (p. 99).

similar.q: It rained a lot; ___, they had fun.

questions.q: Sensible people are ...
why: People who are practical and think a lot are called sensible (p. 101).

similar.q: Modest people are ...

questions.q: Which word comes first in a dictionary?
why: All start with de-.
Compare the third letters: a (dear) comes before l, n, s (p. 101).
questions.tip: Look at the first letter that is different.

similar.q: Which comes first: 'bus' or 'bull'?

questions.q: If you are being bullied, it is your fault.
why: The text says it's not your fault; the person bullying has the problem (p. 104).
questions.tip: Bullying is never the victim's fault.

similar.q: Should you ignore bullying?

questions.q: Filmon is strong. He ___ help.
why: can + verb shows ability (p. 106).
questions.tip: can + base verb (no to, no s).

similar.q: Is he ___ to walk on his own?

questions.q: What should come first in a descriptive paragraph?
why: The first step is to write a topic sentence that introduces the topic (p. 108).

similar.q: Name two things to include when you describe a person.

questions.q: This is one of ___ dresses I have ever seen. (beautiful)
why: Long adjective, superlative: the most beautiful (p. 109).

similar.q: What do you consider ___ in life? (difficult)

questions.q: You must be ___ than I thought. (patient)
why: Two-syllable word, comparing two: more patient (p. 109).

similar.q: I am ___ than my niece. (young)

questions.q: "Our neighbour Sennay, who studied economics, is dining with us." The clause is ...
why: It gives extra information between commas (p. 115).

similar.q: "This is the house that I told you about." Defining or non-defining?

questions.q: Kaleb cut ___ when he was shaving.
why: Kaleb is a man: he → himself (p. 113).
questions.tip: Match the reflexive to the subject.

similar.q: She taught ___ to play the piano.

questions.q: What caused Helen Keller's disabilities?
why: At 19 months she had a high fever which made her deaf and blind (p. 116).

similar.q: Who was Helen's teacher?

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
why: like is not used in the -ing form (p. 118).
like always has an object: it.

similar.q: Correct it: "She like chocolate."

units.title: Resources and Our Future
units.intro: We talk about **resources** in Eritrea, population, recycling, extreme places and **water**. Grammar: much / many, too / enough, the second conditional with would / could / might, and the future simple.

cards.title: What are resources?
body: Resources are things we need and use: water, food, fuel, electricity, wood.
Different places have different resources.
Put the resources in your area in **order of priority** (importance).

cards.title: Four places in Eritrea
head: Place
Scarce
Available
rows: fish, rice, pasta, clean water from wells
all kinds of food, charcoal, 24-hour electricity
bamia, onions, wine, buses, mobile phones, electricity

cards.title: Erafaile
paras: Erafaile is on the coast of the Northern Red Sea, so there is fish to eat.
Vegetables and dairy products are **scarce**. There is no electricity, but the clinic has solar power.
Trees are becoming **rare** because many have been cut down.
People cook with wood and charcoal. Other fuels are not available.

questions.q: Why is there fish in Erafaile?
What does the clinic use for power?
Why are trees becoming rare?

cards.meaning: not enough; hard to find
cards.example: Vegetables and dairy products are [[scarce]].

cards.meaning: not found often
cards.example: The dugong is a [[rare]] sea animal in Eritrea's Red Sea.

cards.meaning: to give something to many people
cards.example: Every year, exercise books are [[distributed]] by the school administrator.

cards.meaning: if not
cards.example: [[Unless]] we use resources carefully, we will face problems.

cards.title: A report in three paragraphs
body: 1. How does my family use resources **now**?
2. How will my family **improve** our resource use in the future?
3. How will the resources in my area **change** in the future?

cards.title: A model report (short)
cards.task: Write a report in three paragraphs about resources in your family and your area.
model: **Now:** We use too much water. We throw away a big bag of rubbish every day.
**Improve:** We will take fewer showers and baths. We will keep bottles and bags to use again.
**Change:** I think water will be available for a long time if we use it carefully.
body: Sentences from the book's model report (p. 124).

cards.title: much and many
rule: **much** + uncountable nouns (water, money, work).
**many** + countable nouns (bananas, people, students).

examples.text: I don't have [[much]] money.
I don't have [[many]] bananas.
There are too [[much]] people here.

cards.title: too and enough
rule: **Enough** and **too** are opposites. **Too** is always negative (more than we want).

examples.text: There is [[too much]] work and [[not enough]] time.
There is [[too much]] rain so there is a flood.
There isn't water [[enough]].

cards.why: We can't count water, so we say much water (p. 125).

cards.title: World population
body: The book's graph shows world population from 1750 to 2150.
The population is **increasing**.
Talk about the advantages and disadvantages of fast population growth, and the effect on resources.

cards.title: A large family or a small family?
cards.task: Choose a picture. Add three or four sentences to the dialogue. Use the word **urgent**.

lines.text: The baby is due next week. How will we feed another child?
I don't know. We need food for the children. This is not enough.
We need an urgent solution.
Let's go to the clinic and ask about family planning.

body: The first three lines are from the book's cartoon (p. 128).

cards.meaning: needing action now
cards.example: We need an [[urgent]] solution.

cards.title: Second conditional with would, could, might
rule: **If + past tense, modal + infinitive**. It describes an unlikely or impossible situation.
**would** = more likely. **could / might** = less likely.

examples.text: If you [[ate]] this spoiled food, you [[would get]] ill.
If the population decreased, science [[could slow down]].
If resources were not managed well, we [[might not have]] enough.
If you [[eat]] this spoiled food, you would get ill.
examples.fix: If you [[ate]] this spoiled food, you would get ill.

cards.title: The language of discussion
cards.task: Prepare an argument for one opinion about population growth.

lines.text: What do you think of family planning?
Umm, I think it should be promoted.
To my mind, population growth is dangerous.
I think we should take care of resources.

body: Use I think or To my mind before your opinion (p. 132).

cards.meaning: to stop something from happening
cards.example: If we don't [[cease]] population growth, the planet will be destroyed.

cards.meaning: to say what will happen
cards.example: The government [[predicts]] population will grow fast.

cards.title: Recycling
paras: "Throwaway societies are a **formula** for disaster."
Using things again is called **recycling**. It is a great way of taking care of resources.
It is also good **finance**: you don't spend money on new things.
For example, bottles for Coca Cola can take drinking water to school.

questions.q: What is recycling?
Why is recycling good finance?
questions.a: You don't spend money on new things.

cards.meaning: with rules that must be obeyed
cards.example: There are [[strict]] rules in our village about cutting down trees.

cards.meaning: before; earlier
cards.example: The [[former]] use of the bottles was for holding Coca Cola.

cards.meaning: a way to get a result
cards.example: Hard work and good health are a [[formula]] for success.

cards.title: The Arctic
paras: The Arctic is very cold: from −40 °C to 0 °C. Trees and plants can't grow.
People eat meat: seal, whale, deer, polar bear and walrus.
They wear animal skins. They make **flames** with oil from seal fat.
The traditional house is the **igloo**, made from blocks of ice. It is warm inside.

questions.q: Why can't plants grow in the Arctic?
What is an igloo made of?

cards.title: The Sahara Desert
paras: In the Sahara it can be below freezing at night and very hot in the day.
People find an **oasis** (a place with plants and water) to rest and get water.
They eat rice, dates, and sheep and camel meat.
Many are **nomads**. They live in tents and travel on foot or by camel.
They wear white, loose clothes and turbans.

questions.q: What is an oasis?
questions.a: A place in a desert with plants and water.

questions.q: Why are camels good for the desert?
questions.a: They can travel a long way with little water.

cards.meaning: another thing you can use instead
cards.example: An [[alternative]] to a stone house is an igloo.

cards.meaning: difficult, but it tests you
cards.example: The lowlands in Eritrea are [[challenging]] because it is very hot.

cards.title: Water
paras: Earth is the only planet with life. Our most important resource is water.
Our bodies are 65% water. Humans die after two or three days without water.
By 2025, 48 countries with 3 billion people will have scarce water.
In Lake Victoria, population growth, over-fishing and pollution threaten the environment.
Solutions: keep water clean, manage fishing and industry, and control population growth.

questions.q: How long can humans live without water?
What percentage of our bodies is water?
Give one solution from the text.
questions.a: Keep water clean / keep waste far from water / manage fishing and industry.

cards.meaning: to be made of
cards.example: A tomato [[consists of]] 95% water.

cards.meaning: something very important that comes first
cards.example: One of our [[priorities]] is to stop people cutting down trees.

cards.title: Future simple: will / will not
rule: **will + verb** describes planned actions in the future.
Negative: **will not** (won't) + verb.

examples.text: I [[will collect]] dead wood for fires.
I [[will not damage]] trees.
I [[will collects]] dead wood.

cards.title: Library skills
body: Choose a topic: global warming, drought, renewable energy, fossil fuels, family planning or recycling.
Find information in reference books.
Write **notes** (words or short phrases), not sentences.
Then present your information to the class.

cards.title: Editing and proofreading
body: Read your report carefully.
Check spelling, punctuation, capital letters and grammar.
Ask your partner to check it. Then write the final report neatly.

too = more than we want; not enough = less than we need.

items.why: Second conditional: past tense after if.

items.text: An igloo is made from blocks of ice.
In Erafaile there is fish to eat.

questions.q: In Erafaile, which resources are scarce?
why: The text says vegetables and dairy products are scarce (p. 122).

similar.q: Why is there fish in Erafaile?

questions.q: In Asmara, water is ___ to people's houses by truck.
why: The Asmara text says water is delivered to other houses by water trucks (p. 122).

why: unless = if not (p. 123).
questions.tip: Unless + good action → otherwise a bad result.

similar.q: To protect our resources, people should ___ be careful with water.

questions.q: How many paragraphs does the model report have?
why: Now / improve / change in the future: three paragraphs (p. 124).

similar.q: What is the first paragraph about?
similar.a: how the family uses resources now

cards.title: The origin of money
paras: Long ago people traded things they had for things they wanted. This is called **barter**.
Barter had problems. Mangoes and shoes were not **equivalent**, and mangoes can spoil.
People used teeth, spices, leather, rocks, gold, silver and cowrie shells as money.
But gold is heavy to **transfer** and hard to divide. So people had the idea of paper money.
People liked gold because it is attractive and it **resists corrosion**.
Researchers think wealthy people in Mesopotamia used money at least as early as 2500 B.C.

I [[am able to]] draw pictures.
[[Unless]] someone helps me, I can't draw people.
I'm [[unable paint]].

cards.title: Emotions in film and theatre
body: "The woman is **sad** because she is crying. The man is **sensitive** because he is comforting her."
Look at **facial expressions** and **body language** to see emotions.

cards.meaning: to show a feeling or moment exactly

cards.meaning: a big difference between two things

cards.title: What makes good music?
paras: There are many kinds of music: traditional, blues, hip-hop, rock, rap and pop.
A good song is a matter of personal opinion. There is no **formula** for good music.
To describe music, talk about the **beat** (drums), the **lyrics** (words), the **melody** (tune) and the **feeling**.

questions.q: What things can we mention when discussing music?
questions.a: The beat, the lyrics, the melody and the feeling.

questions.q: Is there a formula for good music?
All traditional Eritrean songs are about being always happy. True or false?
questions.a: False: the writer says most lyrics are.

cards.title: Describing a song I like
cards.task: Describe a song you like and explain why.
model: I like traditional Eritrean songs due to many factors. **First**, they use traditional drum beats which make them good to dance to.
**Second**, most lyrics are about being always happy even when life is hard. **Third**, they are fast and make me feel hopeful.
**In addition**, they use a catchy melody so that I can sing along. **For these reasons** I like traditional songs.
body: The book's own model (pp. 186–187).

cards.title: Relativity by M.C. Escher
paras: **Relativity** (1953) was drawn by the famous Dutch artist M.C. Escher.
His pictures often show images which are physically impossible in our **universe**.
Escher was not a mathematician, but some of his paintings are mathematically **perfect**.

questions.q: Who drew Relativity?
What do his pictures often show?
questions.a: Images which are physically impossible in our universe.

cards.meaning: to explain the meaning of something

cards.meaning: with no mistakes

cards.title: How to draw an elephant
cards.task: Put the instructions in order using First, Secondly, Thirdly, Next, Finally.
model: **First**, use a pencil to draw a big oval for the body and a small overlapping circle for the head.
**Secondly**, draw four slightly curved rectangles for the legs. Then add two triangles for the ears.
**Thirdly**, add curved lines for the tail and trunk. Then add two curved shapes for the tusks.
**Next**, draw ovals for the eyes and curved lines for the mouth.
**Finally**, use a pen to draw over the lines you want and erase the pencil lines.
body: The book's paragraphs in the correct order: e, a, d, b, c (pp. 189–190).

cards.meaning: exactly, without any change
cards.example: Follow the instructions [[strictly]] to draw an elephant.

cards.title: Ancient art
paras: Cave paintings are paintings on cave walls. Most were made in **prehistoric** times, before written history.
Most are 10,000–20,000 years old. The oldest ones in the text are from 33,000 years ago.
Nobody knows why people painted them. Most show animals or hunting scenes.
About 350 caves have paintings, many in France and Spain. Paintings of animals were found in Danakil, Eritrea.
Erosion and people can damage them. We all must protect these old works of art.

cards.title: A natural musician
paras: Mozart was a famous **composer** (someone who writes music). He was born in 1756 and died in 1791.
By the time he was 5, he **had already started** writing songs. Before 8, he **had performed** concerts in Europe.
At 14 he stopped performing and studied for three years. In 1773 he started to tour again.

questions.q: When was Mozart born?

questions.a: He had already started writing songs.

cards.title: Past perfect
rule: Use **had + past participle** for the earlier past event.

I [[hadn't read]] a book by the time I was one year old.
By the time he was 5, he [[has started]] writing songs.

lines.text: Oh no! Look over there! Can you see the flames? We should help.
I think a spark from the cooking fire blew into the wood. I can't stop it.
We'll help – where are your buckets?
Thank you for your help. At least we are safe.
I'm lucky to have such good friends.

The story is [[imaginative]], the jokes are [[funny]] and even the animation is [[fantastic]].
This movie is full of laughs and jokes for all the family. Watch it soon!
body: A review gives an **opinion**. This one is **positive** (p. 197).

body: What it is about (a short summary).
Your **opinion**: is it good or bad? Why?
Positive words: great, fun, fantastic, enjoyable.
A recommendation: Watch it soon!
