units.title: Creative Words
units.intro: We read **creative writing**: poems, fables, a short story, limericks, a novel and a legend. Grammar: **a / the**, story tenses, **relative clauses** and reported speech. Last, exam techniques.

cards.meaning: good at making or inventing new things
cards.example: She is a [[creative]] person.
body: The verb **create** means make / invent.

options.A: You need to use creative thinking.

cards.why: creative is an adjective, so it needs a noun after it: creative thinking (p. 200).

cards.title: Reading is good for you
body: Think of three ways reading can help you.
Do television programmes give you as much pleasure and information as reading?

cards.title: Love poem for my country
cards.source: Love poem for my country (adapted from Sandile Dikene)
paras: Verse 1: My country is for **love**: valleys, ancient rivers and birds in the sky.
Verse 2: My country is for **joy**: mountains, baboons hopping, heights and rocks.
Verse 3: My country is for **health and wealth**: the blue sea, fish, and a worker's golden voice.
Verse 4: My country is for **all**: millions of people with joined hands and hope in their eyes. "We shall celebrate."

questions.q: What is each verse about?
questions.a: Love, joy, health and wealth, and all the people.

questions.q: What does 'celebrate' mean in the last line?

cards.meaning: to enjoy yourself and be happy on a special occasion
cards.example: There is hope in their eyes. We shall [[celebrate]].

cards.title: What is a fable?
body: A **fable** is a brief story that seems to be about animals but teaches us about ourselves.
A fable always has a **moral** (a lesson on how to behave).
Aesop, who lived in Greece around 600 BC, wrote famous fables.

cards.title: The fisherman and the small fish
cards.source: The fisherman and the small fish (Aesop)
paras: A fisherman caught one very small fish. The fish asked him to throw it back into the sea.
"When I become a big fish, you can catch me again. Then I will make a better meal."
The fisherman laughed: "A small meal today is better than taking a chance on a bigger meal later."

questions.q: What is the moral?
questions.a: Sometimes it's better to be satisfied with what you have.

cards.title: The fox and the crow
paras: A crow found a piece of cheese and flew with it into a tree.
A fox wanted the cheese. She said the crow was beautiful and asked him to sing one song.
The crow was pleased and began to sing. The cheese fell out of his mouth, and the clever fox ate it.

questions.q: Why did the fox praise the crow?
What happened when the crow sang?
questions.a: The cheese fell out of his mouth and the fox ate it.

cards.title: a and the
rule: Use **a** the first time something is mentioned.
Use **the** when it is mentioned again.

examples.text: I read [[a]] book. [[The]] book was very interesting.
One day [[a]] lion was sleeping. [[A]] little mouse ran across his leg. This woke [[the]] lion.
I am going to write [[the]] poem. [[A]] poem will be about nature.
examples.fix: I am going to write [[a]] poem. [[The]] poem will be about nature.
examples.note: First time: a. Mentioned again: the.

cards.title: The dream
paras: Amina had a very clear dream. She was in a large crowd of women and children moving slowly down a road towards the mountains.
The next day was normal, but she was a little quieter than usual.
The second night she was alone on the road. It led to a door between two stone pillars.
On the third night she went to bed late. In the dream she reached out to push open the door. She had no choice.

questions.q: What does 'it' in the first line refer to?
Which word is closest in meaning to emotion?
Why was Amina quieter than usual?
questions.a: She was thinking about her strange dream.

cards.meaning: a feeling
cards.example: They were moving slowly down a road, without showing any [[emotion]].

cards.title: Three story tenses
rule: **Past simple**: the main events. **Past continuous**: an action in progress.
**Past perfect**: an event before another past event.

examples.text: Amina [[woke]] early. (past simple)
They [[were moving]] slowly down a road. (past continuous)
She [[had been]] one of a large crowd. (past perfect)
He [[has got]] off the train to buy some water before it left.
examples.fix: He [[had got]] off the train to buy some water.

cards.title: A story in the right order
cards.task: Put the sentences in order. Sentence c is first.
model: I [[was sitting]] on a train with my family. We [[were travelling]] to the airport to start a new life in England.
The journey took many hours as the train stopped many times. It was a hot day and we were very thirsty.
Suddenly we saw that my father was not sitting with us. He [[had got]] off the train to buy some water.
The train [[had started]] before he got back on. It was an awful situation. We were very worried.
He [[had taken]] a faster train. We arrived at the airport. You can imagine our relief when we saw our father waiting for us.
phrases: You can imagine our relief when ...
body: The book's sentences in order: c, f, a, d, b, e (p. 207). Plan: people, place, what happens, conclusion.

cards.meaning: very bad
cards.example: It was an [[awful]] situation. We were very worried.

cards.meaning: a happy feeling when a worry ends
cards.example: You can imagine our [[relief]] when we saw our father.

cards.title: Rhyme
body: **Rhyme** happens when the final syllables of words sound the same.
*dog* rhymes with *log*; *boy* rhymes with *toy*.

cards.title: A limerick
cards.task: Write your own limerick with your partner: There was a young student from ...
model: There was a young boy called [[Batton]]
Who went to bed with his hat [[on]].
"If I wake up," he [[said]]
"With my hat on my [[head]],
I'll know that it hasn't been sat [[on]]."
body: A limerick is a short funny poem of **5 lines**. Lines 1, 2 and 5 rhyme; lines 3 and 4 rhyme (pp. 208–209).

cards.title: Check your limerick
body: 5 lines?
Lines 1, 2 and 5 rhyme?
Lines 3 and 4 rhyme?
Is it funny?

rule: A relative clause follows a noun and gives information about it.

Charlotte Bronte[[, who lived in the 19th century,]] wrote the book. (non-defining)

Don't keep your feelings in. Talking opens your mind and often solves problems.

questions.a: Talking to family or friends when you feel bad.

questions.q: Who can you talk to?

rule: Statements: **said that** + past. Questions: **asked + what / if**. Orders: **told + person + to**.

examples.note: Reported question: normal word order, past tense.

cards.title: What is a legend?
body: A **legend** is a story from ancient times.
It may begin with a true event, but people add exciting details over the years.

cards.title: The Giraffe in the sky
cards.source: The Giraffe in the sky (an African legend)
paras: At the beginning the sun was **naughty** and kept getting lost in the sky.
The Creator gave Giraffe a job: to follow and **chase** the sun. The sun never got lost again.
To honour Giraffe, the Creator made a giraffe shape with stars. Some African people call it Tutwa.
English speaking people call it the Southern Cross. People use it to guide them at night.

questions.q: Name a true fact in the legend.
questions.a: The star pattern can be seen in the Southern Hemisphere and guides travellers.

questions.q: Name an imaginary fact.
questions.a: Giraffe chased the sun so it did not get lost.
